rv.q: As a play, though, “Corruption” is uncompelling — counterintuitively so, given the inherent drama: the crimes, the coverup, the comeuppance (or not), the clashes of personality.
The problem is a failure to access any part of us below the neck.
Rogers and Sher can take responsibility and credit for one of the season’s few must-sees.

Corruption doesn’t succeed as fully as Oslo because it’s a more complex, elongated story featuring so many characters that nearly every cast member, with the exceptions of Stephens and Burrows, play multiple roles.
It remains more a cerebral than an emotional exercise
While the play is somewhat difficult to follow with all of the data, characters and facts, Sher’s production of J.T. Rogers’ complex docudrama is fascinating if low-key in its concept.
Corruption is trying to be multiple things at once, and thus doesn't excel as any of them.
Even if Corruption is a mixed bag, the real-life Watson must be pleased that after years of getting slagged off in the press, an admiring playwright prints the last word.
...a well-intentioned retelling of a troubling episode in the history of news gathering
Ultimately, “Corruption” felt like too much information about an old news story not worth the investment of time and attention, despite the implicit argument about its continuing relevance.
Whether they make for great theater, however, is less certain.
The multifaceted story barrels forward swiftly but clearly.
This is a timely story with a whole lot to say, but the cumulative effect is mostly exhausting.

Corruption is a taut cloak-and-dagger-style drama that makes a bold statement about where we are as a society as technology offers opportunities for abuse in the name of leverage, control, and domination.

cn.t: Rogers' historical drama about the British phone-hacking scandal earns mixed reviews. Critics praise the sophisticated storytelling and strong performances, but many find the subject matter less gripping than his previous work Oslo.
